note: The textbook mentions turkey tail only in passing: a matting species whose blocks set hard if left too long, and the Cap n Stem strain that flew to the space station. Everything else in this drawing (the bag, the slits and how the brackets look as they grow) is general knowledge, not from the sources, and not a growing method.

stages.a: In this drawing: a fully colonized block in a closed bag, cut with two long slits across one face.
stages.v: A matting species: blocks left too long become extremely hard.

stages.a: Rounded white knobs push out of the slits and fuse together. Most become shelves; a few stay small.
The knobs flatten into small white shelves that grow outward from the slit, not upward.
Behind the pale growing edge, rings of colour form one at a time from the base out. The shelves overlap like roof shingles.
Thin, flexible brackets with all their colour zones, and only a narrow pale rim left at the edge.
The edge has stopped growing. Margins curl under, the brackets dry stiff and leathery, and the colours fade. Seen low, from the side.

labels.a: In this drawing, two long slits cut across the bag face; the brackets grow from them.
The whole block is bound into one tough white mat.
labels.v: Turkey tail blocks left too long become extremely hard and difficult to break up.

labels.a: A closed grow bag with a filter patch.
White knobs crowding out of the slit, some fused into lumps. The rest stay as the lumpy base the shelves grow from.
Young shelves: thick, white and rounded, growing out flat.
A pale band along the margin: the part still growing. It narrows as the bracket finishes.
Concentric bands of brown, rust, grey and blue, darker and lighter by turns, parallel to the edge.
Brackets overlap like roof shingles, row over row.
Fine hairs make every other band velvety; the bands between are smoother.
No gills: the white underside is covered in tiny pores.
A thin, wavy edge, often lobed.
The edge curls under and dries tough and leathery.
Fine white spores drift down from the pores.
